summaries.example: Imagine an app that chooses which videos to show you. The people who designed it made some choices, and the company decided to use it. You also choose what to watch. If the app causes harm, it may be too simple to blame only the app or only one person. We may need to ask what each person did, what the app made easier or harder, and whether anyone could have noticed the danger.
summaries.summary: Computers are part of many human activities, so figuring out who is morally responsible can be difficult. Moral responsibility usually connects an agent—the person or group acting—with a patient—the person or thing affected. We often look for three conditions: a person must have some causal connection to the result, be able to think about possible consequences, and have some freedom to choose. Computing can make each condition harder to judge. A system may be built by many people, used far away, and operate for years after its designers act. It may also hide how it reaches a result, causing people to trust it too much or too little. Computer systems can guide, limit, or encourage choices, but they do not automatically control everything people do. Philosophers disagree about whether advanced computers could become moral agents. Others say computers are not responsible agents but are still important parts of human moral action. The entry also presents approaches that emphasize positive duties, shared accountability, and meaningful human control over technological systems.
key_ideas: Responsibility usually involves three questions: Did someone help cause the outcome? Could they understand possible consequences? Could they choose how to act?
Computers can influence people’s choices without making every choice for them.
Many people may help design, sell, manage, and use one system. This is called the problem of many hands.
A computer may follow rules or make choices, but philosophers disagree about whether it can truly be morally responsible.
Responsibility can look backward, asking who was at fault, or forward, asking who should prevent harm.
Good responsibility practices should focus not only on blame but also on preventing foreseeable harm.
summaries.why_it_matters: Computers help decide what we see, buy, receive, or are asked to do. If no one accepts responsibility when a system causes harm, people may not fix the problem or protect others. Thinking carefully about responsibility can help designers, users, companies, and public organizations make safer systems and respond fairly when things go wrong.

important_terms.definition: When we say a person deserves praise or blame for what they did and what happened because of it.
A person or group that does something. In a computer system, many agents may help create or use it.
A person, group, or thing affected by an action.
The link between an action and what happens afterward.
The ability to choose and control what you do instead of being completely forced.
When people rely too much, or too little, on what a computer system says.

questions_to_think_about: If a computer makes a harmful mistake, who should investigate it?
Can a tool influence your choice without forcing you?
Why might it be unfair to blame only the person nearest to a computer system?
What should designers do when they cannot predict every way a system will be used?

summaries.example: Suppose a public agency uses an algorithm to help decide who receives a benefit. The system was designed by programmers, shaped by managers and policy makers, trained on data, and used by officials. A person denied the benefit may not know how the result was produced, while the officials may have little ability to change it. Responsibility cannot be settled simply by blaming the computer or the nearest employee. A careful analysis asks whether the system tracked the relevant reasons and facts, whether its outcome can be traced to human decisions, and which participants had knowledge, control, and opportunities to act differently.
summaries.summary: The entry examines how computing unsettles familiar ideas about moral responsibility. Traditional approaches commonly ask whether an agent caused an outcome, could reasonably understand its consequences, and was free enough to act otherwise. Computerized activity often takes place in sociotechnical systems: people and institutions work together with artifacts that shape perception, choices, and available actions. This creates the problem of many hands, while distance, delayed effects, system opacity, and automation bias make causal and epistemic judgments harder. Automation can also reduce the discretion of human operators, raising questions about autonomy and where responsibility moves within an organization. The entry reviews competing responses. Some theorists explore whether sufficiently autonomous and intentional artificial systems could count as moral agents, while critics stress that current systems lack capacities associated with human moral agency. Other views treat artifacts as morally relevant mediators without making them responsible agents. Further proposals rethink responsibility as a forward-looking professional duty, a culture of accountability, or a distributed practice. The idea of meaningful human control requires sociotechnical systems both to track relevant moral reasons and facts and to trace outcomes to human decisions capable of answering for them. No single consensus resolves these disputes, but responsible analysis must include both human conduct and technological mediation.
key_ideas: Conventional accounts often connect responsibility to causal influence, knowledge of consequences, and freedom or autonomy. Computing complicates all three.
The problem of many hands, organizational complexity, temporal distance, and physical distance can obscure how actions contribute to outcomes.
Computer systems can expand knowledge by analyzing information, but opacity and automation bias can also limit users’ understanding and judgment.
Technologies mediate action: their designs embody choices and values, while their meaning and effects depend partly on human use and context. They influence action without necessarily determining it.

Some philosophers defend the possibility of artificial moral agents; others argue that current computers lack intentionality, understanding, sentience, or the autonomy required for moral responsibility.
Alternative approaches emphasize positive responsibility, accountability as a social practice, distributed agency, and meaningful human control through tracking and tracing.
summaries.why_it_matters: Computing now participates in decisions and actions whose effects may be widespread, delayed, opaque, and difficult to reverse. If responsibility is assigned too narrowly, organizations may evade duties; if it is assigned to the nearest operator, that person may become a convenient but unfair target. The philosophical debate helps clarify what designers, users, managers, policy makers, and institutions should know, control, anticipate, and do to reduce harm.

important_terms.definition: A normative relation in which an agent may appropriately be praised or blamed for a morally significant outcome, often because the agent acted voluntarily and had relevant control or knowledge.
The capacity to originate morally significant action and, in many accounts, to deliberate, choose, and act with relevant autonomy.
The contribution that links an action or decision to a later outcome; computing often distributes this link across people, organizations, and artifacts.
The difficulty of assigning responsibility when many people contribute to a system and no single contribution appears sufficient to produce the outcome.
A tendency to trust automated outputs too much or too little, which can weaken human judgment and awareness of consequences.
A forward-looking form of responsibility centered on attending to consequences and working to prevent foreseeable harm, rather than only assigning blame afterward.
A proposed condition for responsible sociotechnical design: system behavior should reflect relevant human reasons and facts, and outcomes should be traceable to earlier human decisions.
The idea that moral action and responsibility may be spread across human actors and the technologies that shape their choices, rather than located in one individual alone.

questions_to_think_about: Does causal contribution require direct control, or can a person be responsible for designing conditions that later shape an outcome?
When does reliance on an opaque automated system become negligent rather than reasonable?
Would calling a computer accountable help address harm, or could it distract from the humans and institutions behind it?
How should responsibility be distributed when an outcome results from interacting technical and organizational decisions?
What would it mean for a system to track human reasons and for an outcome to be traceable to human choices?

summaries.example: A school uses software to flag students who may need extra support. The program was built by a company, chosen by school leaders, trained with data, and interpreted by counselors. A counselor might trust the result, even though the program’s reasoning is hard to see. If a student is wrongly flagged, it may be unfair to blame only the counselor or say, “The computer did it.” We should ask who helped create the system, who understood its limits, who could check the result, and who had a chance to correct the mistake.
summaries.summary: Computers complicate moral responsibility because they are woven into human decisions rather than serving only as simple tools. Moral responsibility usually involves a causal connection to an outcome, the ability to consider possible consequences, and enough freedom to choose. Digital systems can make these conditions difficult to evaluate. Many contributors may design, test, regulate, sell, maintain, and use one system. Effects may occur far away or years later. Users may not understand hidden calculations, and they may either trust an automated answer too much or ignore it too much. Computing can also guide behavior by limiting choices, offering nudges, or standardizing decisions. These influences raise questions about human autonomy, but the entry notes that technology normally shapes action without determining it completely. Philosophers disagree about whether computers could count as moral agents. Some focus on possible artificial agency; others say computers lack key human capacities and should instead be understood as morally relevant parts of systems involving people. Proposals for dealing with responsibility include positive duties to prevent harm, shared accountability, and designs that preserve meaningful human control. The central lesson is that responsibility should be studied across the whole human-technology setting, not assigned automatically to one person or to the machine.
key_ideas: Philosophers often connect responsibility with influence over an outcome, knowledge of possible consequences, and freedom to choose.
Computing can spread responsibility across designers, programmers, managers, sellers, users, and organizations.
Technology can shape decisions by making some actions easier, harder, more noticeable, or less noticeable, while still leaving room for human interpretation and choice.
Automated systems may help people understand information, but hidden processes can also make it difficult to judge whether the system is reliable.
There is disagreement about whether future computers could be moral agents. Many critics say current computers do not have the understanding, intentions, or autonomy needed for that status.
Some philosophers recommend looking at responsibility as a continuing social practice: people and organizations should answer for systems, improve them, and prevent future harm.
summaries.why_it_matters: Algorithms and other computer systems can affect education, work, public services, communication, and safety. Understanding responsibility helps people ask better questions: Who designed the rules? Who checked the risks? Who can explain or change the result? Who must respond when the system harms someone? These questions support fairer decisions and more reliable technology.

important_terms.definition: Being appropriately praised or blamed for an action or its morally important result.
The person or group that acts or helps bring about an outcome.
The person, group, or thing affected by an action.
A connection between what someone does and what happens later.
The ability to understand possible results and make a choice without being completely forced.
A difficulty that appears when many people contribute to one system, making it hard to tell who is responsible for which part.
A habit of trusting or distrusting automated advice too much.
Responsibility understood as a duty to consider effects and help prevent harm, not just a way to decide who deserves blame afterward.

questions_to_think_about: If several people each make a small contribution to a harmful result, can more than one person be responsible?
Should a designer be responsible for uses of a system that were difficult to predict?
How can people keep meaningful control when software makes decisions automatically?
Is blaming a computer ever a useful explanation, or does it usually hide human choices?
What information should a user have before relying on an automated recommendation?
